catalog.name: GitHub
catalog.description: Issues, PRs, code search and git.
catalog.hint: Any repo-scoped token is enough: the agent calls the API with curl, and with Git access on, pull and push work over HTTPS. The two extra permissions beside add native ssh://git and CI webhooks on workspace repos — without them both still work, and the card shows you what to add by hand.

guide.scopes: `repo` (+ `write:public_key` for native ssh, `admin:repo_hook` for CI webhooks)
steps: Open `Settings` → `Developer settings` → `Personal access tokens`.
Classic: generate a token with the `repo` scope (add `write:public_key` for native `ssh://git`, `admin:repo_hook` for CI webhooks).
Fine-grained: grant repo `Contents` access (add the `Git SSH keys: write` account permission for native `ssh://git`, and `Webhooks: write` for CI).
Copy the token and paste it here. Git works over HTTPS regardless; the extra permissions only enable native ssh and automatic CI webhooks.

catalog.name: GitLab
catalog.description: Issues, merge requests, pipelines and git.
catalog.hint: The api scope covers both extras: an SSH key on your account for ssh://git, and a CI webhook on workspace repos. If key upload is refused git is rerouted over HTTPS; the webhook also needs the token's user to be at least Maintainer. Either way the card shows what to add by hand.

steps: Self-hosted: set the `Instance URL` above first.
Open `User settings` → `Access tokens`.
Add a token with the `api` scope.
Copy the token and paste it here.

catalog.name: npm
catalog.description: Publish and manage packages on npm.
catalog.hint: The agent uses the npm CLI, already signed in. Publishing may ask for a one-time 2FA code: with a TOTP secret stored, the agent mints its own and never sees the secret. Write tokens expire within 90 days — paste a fresh one under Sandbox ▸ Secrets.

guide.scopes: granular access token: `Read and write` on the packages/scopes the agent manages
steps: Sign in on npmjs.com, click your avatar → `Access Tokens` → `Generate New Token` → `Granular Access Token` (classic tokens no longer exist).
Grant `Read and write` on just the packages or scopes the agent should manage, pick the expiry deliberately (write tokens live at most `90 days`, `7` by default), and paste the token here.

Publishing enforces 2FA: either enable `Bypass 2FA` on the token (npm is narrowing this to staging a publish you then approve on the site), or store your TOTP secret below so the agent can answer OTP prompts.
The TOTP secret is the base32 key behind your authenticator's QR code (`Can't scan the QR code?` at enrollment). Only accounts already on TOTP have one — npm no longer offers new TOTP enrollments.
On WebAuthn instead of TOTP (npm's default now)? Add the `npmjs.com` browser card too: the sandbox enrolls its own passkey there and answers 2FA prompts and publish approvals itself.

fields.label: 2FA TOTP secret
fields.hint: Never shown to the agent — it mints expiring codes from it instead. Leave empty if your account uses WebAuthn/passkeys or publishing rides a Bypass-2FA token.

catalog.name: npmjs.com
catalog.description: Your npm account in a real browser.
catalog.hint: Use Log in to sign in once. A physical security key cannot reach this browser — sign in with a recovery code instead, then open npm's 2FA settings and `Add Security Key`: the sandbox enrolls its own passkey and answers every later 2FA prompt itself. Pairs with the npm connector — its publishes get their web approvals here.

catalog.name: Browser session
catalog.description: Sign into any site; the agent acts as you.
catalog.hint: The card for sites that have no card — an internal admin panel, a supplier portal, a client's CMS. Every other browser card is this one with the addresses filled in and a site cheatsheet attached, so use those where they exist: they teach the agent the site's own URLs and controls, which this one has to discover by reading the page. Add one session per account, named after the account.

fields.label: Page to open
fields.hint: Where this account lives once you are signed in — the page you would bookmark.

fields.label: Sign-in page
fields.hint: Only when signing in happens somewhere else (a separate identity provider). Otherwise the page above is where the login window opens.

fields.label: What you will use it for
fields.placeholder: read and reply to supplier tickets
fields.hint: One line, in your words. This is what tells the agent when to reach for this account instead of another.

catalog.name: Sentry
catalog.description: Query issues and traces from Sentry.
catalog.hint: Self-hosted: set your instance URL above first. Leave the org blank to let the agent list your orgs.

steps: Open `Settings` → `Account` → `Auth Tokens` (or `Developer Settings` → `Internal Integration`).
Create a token with the `project:read`, `event:read` and `org:read` scopes.
Copy the token and paste it here.

catalog.name: Redmine
catalog.description: Issues and projects from your Redmine.
catalog.hint: The agent uses the API key with curl.

guide.scopes: REST API must be enabled by an admin
steps: Set the `Instance URL` above first.
Open `My account` (top-right).
Under `API access key`, click `Show` (an admin enables it in `Administration` → `Settings` → `API` if hidden).
Copy the key and paste it here.

catalog.name: Outline
catalog.description: Docs and knowledge base from Outline.
catalog.hint: The agent uses the token with curl against the Outline API.

steps: Set the `Instance URL` above first.
Open `Settings` → `API Tokens`.
Create a token and give it a name.
Copy the token and paste it here.

catalog.name: Notion
catalog.description: Pages and databases in your Notion workspace.
catalog.hint: The agent calls the Notion API with curl. An integration sees nothing on its own: share pages with it (page `•••` → `Connections`) and everything nested underneath comes along. When the agent reports a page as not found, it is usually one nobody shared.

guide.scopes: Read content — add Update + Insert content for an agent that writes
steps: Open `Settings` → `Connections` → `Develop or manage integrations`, and create a `New integration` — type `Internal`, in the workspace the agent should reach.
Under `Capabilities`, grant `Read content`; add `Update content` and `Insert content` if the agent should write. `No user information` is fine.
Copy the `Internal Integration Secret` and paste it here.
Share content with it: on each top-level page or database, open `•••` → `Connections` and add the integration — sub-pages inherit. Until this step the integration sees nothing at all.

catalog.name: SigNoz
catalog.description: Query traces, logs and metrics from SigNoz.
catalog.hint: The agent queries observability with curl.

steps: Set the `SigNoz URL` above (Cloud or self-hosted).
Open `Settings` → `API Keys` and create a key (`Viewer` role).
Copy the key and paste it here.

catalog.name: Komodo
catalog.description: Drive your Komodo stacks and deployments.
catalog.hint: The agent talks to Komodo Core's HTTP API with curl. A Komodo API key is a key + secret pair — the secret is this card's rotatable credential, the key identifies it (like a database user). The key inherits its user's permissions, so a read-only agent wants a non-admin user.

guide.scopes: the key inherits the user's permissions
steps: Set the `Komodo URL` above first (the address of Komodo Core).
Open your profile (top-right) → `Api Keys` → `New Api Key`.
Komodo shows the key and the secret once — copy both and paste them here.
To keep the agent read-only, make the key on a user that only has `Read` permissions.

catalog.name: PostgreSQL
catalog.description: Query your PostgreSQL database with psql.
catalog.hint: The agent queries your database with psql.

steps: No external token — use an existing DB user, ideally a read-only one.
Make sure the database is reachable from the sandbox (host/port open, grants/`pg_hba` allow it).
PostgreSQL uses port `5432`.
Add this card again with a different name to connect another database.

catalog.name: MySQL
catalog.hint: The agent queries your database with the mysql client.

steps: No external token — use an existing DB user, ideally a read-only one.
Make sure the database is reachable from the sandbox (host/port open, grants allow it).
MySQL uses port `3306`.
Add this card again with a different name to connect another database.

automationTemplates.title: Push to repo
automationTemplates.prompt: A push just landed — the webhook payload is in $AUTOMATION_PAYLOAD. Review the new commits and summarize what changed.
automationTemplates.setup: In the GitHub repo: Settings → Webhooks → Add webhook → paste this URL as the Payload URL, content type application/json. Or from a workflow: put the URL in a secret and add a `uses: intentic/gate-action@v1` step — it sends the event payload for you.

automationTemplates.title: Push to repo
automationTemplates.prompt: A push just landed — the webhook payload is in $AUTOMATION_PAYLOAD. Review the new commits and summarize what changed.
automationTemplates.setup: In the GitLab project: Settings → Webhooks → paste this URL and check Push events.

automationTemplates.title: New alert
automationTemplates.prompt: A Sentry alert just fired — the payload is in $AUTOMATION_PAYLOAD. Investigate the error and suggest a fix.
automationTemplates.setup: In Sentry: Alerts → your alert rule → add a webhook action pointing at this URL.

automationTemplates.title: Deployment alert
automationTemplates.prompt: Komodo just fired an alert — the payload is in $AUTOMATION_PAYLOAD: `level` is the severity, `target` names the resource ({type, id}), `data` carries the specifics, and `resolved` is true when this is the all-clear for an earlier alert. Use your Komodo capability to look up that resource and its recent container logs, then say what broke and what would fix it. Do not deploy, restart or stop anything unless the user asks.
automationTemplates.setup: In Komodo: Alerters → New Alerter → endpoint type Custom → paste this URL. Narrow it with the alerter's alert-type and resource filters.
